Case Information: A 4-year-old boy presented with bilateral cataracts and poor vision. His parents noted that his physical and mental development was typical until he was 2 years old. After that age, he began experiencing difficulties in learning and communicating. Additionally, oculo-digital sign and self-injury behaviors were observed. Ocular B-scan ultrasonography identified retinal detachment in both eyes. Surgical intervention included pars plana vitrectomy and lensectomy in the left eye. Postoperative fundus photographs showed a partially attached retina. The patient's father had physical disabilities due to poliomyelitis but no ophthalmic abnormalities. The mother had phthisis bulbi and keratopathy in the left eye with no light perception, and in the right eye, she had a dragged disk with a visual acuity of 20/125.
Diagnostic Tests: Genetic testing identified a homozygous deletion of exons 2 and 3 in the NDP in the patient.

Case Information: The patient is a 23-year-old female, height 165 cm, weight 36 kg. She exhibited developmental delay at the age of three and cognitive impairment that became noticeable during elementary school, leading to her enrollment in a special school for 12 years with below-average academic performance. At the age of 12, she experienced gait disturbance due to weakness in the right lower extremities. Her medical history includes recurrent abdominal pain, but clinical examinations, blood tests, and abdominal ultrasounds were repeatedly normal. Family history showed no evidence of cerebral, muscle, or cardiac disease, although her parents are first-degree cousins. Her parents, brother, and two sisters showed no phenotypic abnormalities. At the age of 14, a clinical neurological examination revealed startleness without hyperekplexia, social withdrawal, avoidance of eye contact, general wasting, and hyperkyphosis of the thoracic spine. Blood tests showed recurrent mild elevation of creatine-kinase. Needle electromyography results were normal in both weak and non-weak muscles. Nerve conduction studies were normal. A muscle biopsy from the left biceps muscle showed nonspecific changes. Cerebral CT scans were normal. EEG results indicated increased background slowing with diffuse, intermittent theta waves without drowsiness. Neuropsychological testing identified adjustment disorders, anxiety, depression, moderate intellectual disability, a negative self-image, and feelings of being unloved.
Diagnostic Tests: Genetic testing revealed the homozygous variant c.553C>T in exon 6 of the MICU1 gene.

Case Information: A 14-month-old male of Asian and Caucasian descent presented with an 8-month history of recurrent cough, rapid breathing, and low blood oxygen levels, necessitating multiple hospital admissions. He was born full-term with an uncomplicated neonatal period and was of average size for gestational age. Early infancy was notable only for mild eczema, and he received all routine vaccinations. Family history was negative for significant medical or genetic conditions. He lived with both parents and was not on any medications. At 6 months of age, he presented with a 2-week history of dry cough and low oxygen levels, as detected by a home monitoring device (SpO2: 83–91%) at night. Physical examination revealed rapid breathing, subcostal retractions, decreased breath sounds, mild scattered wheezes, and bilateral crackles, without fever. He was treated with antibiotics for bronchiolitis and pneumonia. Despite treatment, he was hospitalized twice for ongoing symptoms of rapid breathing and low oxygen levels, both day and night. He received supplemental oxygen, albuterol, and oral and inhaled steroids. Chest x-ray showed a patchy opacity in the right mid-lung field. Respiratory viral panels were negative, and echocardiogram was normal. Persistent rapid breathing, retractions, and crackles were noted on examination outside of acute respiratory illnesses, with continued reports of nighttime low oxygen levels. A sleep study revealed obstructive sleep apnea (Apnea Hypopnea Index of 5.5) and episodes of persistent low oxygen levels below SpO2 90%. He was referred to a pediatric pulmonologist. Repeat chest x-ray showed patchy ill-defined perihilar opacities. Sweat chloride test and immune work-up were normal. Bronchoscopy with bronchoalveolar lavage was normal.
Diagnostic Tests: The high-resolution CT scan showed areas of mosaic attenuation and geographic ground-glass opacities in a predominant perihilar distribution.

Case Information: A 21-year-old male presented with pain and recurrent nodular swelling over the right foot for the past four years. He works as a farmer. Two years after the onset of painful swellings, there was a history of a sinus from the foot discharging pus with dark-colored granules. The patient had close contact with an active case of pulmonary tuberculosis (his wife). Following the onset of the discharge, the patient visited a local practitioner who sent the pus for culture and sensitivity testing. The patient was started on oral antibiotics based on the sensitivity results. The discharge mildly decreased with oral antibiotics but persisted, and the patient was advised to use local dressings. Due to the persistent discharging sinus, the patient eventually presented to the outpatient department of our hospital. On local examination, multiple nodular swellings were observed over the dorsum, medial, and lateral aspects of the midfoot. There was a discharging sinus over the dorsum of the midfoot, adherent to the bone, with non-undermined margins. There was diffuse tenderness in the mid and forefoot, and movements in these areas were painful and restricted. Blood investigations revealed a marginally high ESR (32) and elevated C-reactive protein levels (20 ng/dl). Plain radiographs of the foot showed multiple lytic lesions involving the metatarso-cuneiform joints and inter-tarsal joints, associated with significant osteoporosis.
Diagnostic Tests: The incisional biopsy was performed from the dorsal aspect of mid foot along with sinus tract excision. The incision revealed pus which was interspersed with dark black coloured granules on gross examination. A big sequestrum was removed from the tarso-metatarsal junction, with multiple black pigmented granules. The histo-pathological examination of the tissue revealed colonies comprising of dense tangled meshwork of slender hyphae interspersed with ovoid to round spore like structures. The colonies had brown pigmentation at the periphery.

Case Information: An 82-year-old man reported experiencing blurred vision and a pressure-like sensation in the left eye for the past year. His medical history included hypertension, glaucoma, and prostate cancer. Visual acuity, corrected to the best possible level, was 20/20 in both eyes. He successfully identified all Ishihara plates with both eyes. Pupil size was 3 mm bilaterally. A grade one relative afferent pupillary defect was noted in the left eye. Examination of the left optic disc revealed mild elevation and indistinct nasal margins, with unobscured blood vessels and no hemorrhages or exudates. Subtle macular edema, a few choroidal folds, and tortuous retinal vessels were observed in the left eye. The right optic disc appeared normal. The remainder of the neuro-ophthalmic examination was unremarkable, with no skin lesions indicative of neurofibromatosis. A central 24–2 threshold Humphrey visual field test showed normal results in both eyes. Macular optical coherence tomography indicated retinal thickening between the optic nerve head and fovea. Lumbar puncture revealed a cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) opening pressure of 90 mm H2O. CSF analysis showed normal cell count and biochemistry, and cytology was negative for malignant cells.
Diagnostic Tests: Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the brain and orbits showed enlarged CSF spaces around the normal appearing left optic nerve. There was no abnormal enhancement of the optic nerve or its sheath. Brain images demonstrated only age-related volume loss.

Case Information: A 42-year-old Japanese woman, who has had one pregnancy and one normal vaginal delivery 13 years ago, showed an increase in uterine size during a screening. She reported recent lower abdominal pain and had been experiencing urinary incontinence and constipation for several months. During a pelvic examination, a fist-sized lump was noted in the uterus and left ovary. The vulva and vagina appeared normal. The portio was not clearly visible, making endometrial smear tests and uteroscopy unfeasible. Serum tumor markers, including carcinoembryonic antigen (CEA), CA125, CA19-9, and squamous cell carcinoma (SCC), were all within normal limits. Human chorionic gonadotropin (hCG) levels were not measured before the operation. An ultrasound showed a cystic mass measuring 125 × 75 mm located behind the uterus, which was interpreted as an endometrioid cyst.
Diagnostic Tests: The MRI showed a solid lesion extending throughout the myometrium of the lower uterine segment and an irregular large cystic lesion filling the pelvic cavity behind the uterus. The solid lesion in the uterus was hyperintense on T2-weighted images (T2WIs), isointense on T1-weighted images (T1WIs) and heterogeneously enhanced on gadolinium-diethylene triamine pentaacetic acid (DTPA)-enhanced T1WI. It appeared hyperintense in diffusion-weighted images (DWIs), with an apparent diffusion coefficient (ADC) value of 0.9 × 10−3 mm2/s. The subserosal cystic lesion had an irregular wall and septum, and protruded into the solid lesion of the posterior wall like an ulceration. The contents of the cystic lesion appeared hyperintense on T2WI, T1WI, and fat suppression T1WI, and included T2WI-hypointense precipitated material. Slightly solid components were present on the inner surface of the cystic wall. There were no findings indicating adenomyosis in the myometrium of the uterus, and no abnormal findings in the endometrium and left ovary. The right ovary was not detected.

Case Information: A 62-year-old male visited the dermatology clinic with multiple discharging sinuses located on the neck and right axillary region, persisting for 2 months. The patient reported a gradual increase in the lesion size with minimal discharge. He denied any history of trauma, fever, weight loss, or tuberculosis. The patient mentioned that he is a retired teacher residing in California for the past decade and travels to India annually. Physical examination revealed multiple discharging sinuses on the anterior neck and right axilla, with mild erythema around the sinus openings and minimal serosanguinous discharge. Systemic examination showed no abnormalities. Laboratory tests, including complete blood count, erythrocyte sedimentation rate, urine routine, renal function test, liver function test, viral markers (HIV, HBsAg, HCV), Mantoux test, and chest X-ray, were all within normal limits.
Diagnostic Tests: The skin biopsy showed normal epidermis and dermis had chronic inflammatory infiltrate comprising of lymphocytes and plasma cells along with noncaseating granulomas. A few thick-walled large round structures were seen, which were present both inside the granulomas and in the surrounding stroma. Periodic Acid Schiff (PAS) stain highlighted these structures and showed globular sporangia with some of them possessing sporangiospores.

Case Information: A 10-month-old girl was brought to the ophthalmic emergency room at King Abdulaziz University Hospital, Riyadh, Kingdom of Saudi Arabia, due to vitreous hemorrhage in the right eye. Her parents had observed an outward deviation of her right eye for the past 5 weeks. They reported no history of ocular or head trauma and no systemic disease. Ophthalmic examination revealed a right exotropia measuring 30 prism diopters. The vision in the right eye was central, steady, and unmaintained, and she resisted occlusion of the left eye. Extra-ocular muscle movements were full. Portable slit-lamp examination of the anterior segment was normal except for mild subconjunctival hemorrhage in the right eye, likely secondary to a previous examination under sedation. Fundus examination of the right eye showed old vitreous hemorrhage covering the macula. There were small saccular dilatations filled with dark blood involving the macula. Slit-lamp and fundus examination of the left eye was normal. She was admitted for further evaluation. General physical examination was normal, and blood work-up did not indicate any bleeding disorders. Brain magnetic resonance imaging was unremarkable with no evidence of subdural hemorrhage or CNS vascular malformation. Bone survey was normal.
Diagnostic Tests: Fundus fluorescein angiography showed delayed filling in the venous phase and lack of leakage in the late phase. Ultrasonography of the right eye showed a dome shaped lesion in the macula that measured 2.5mm in elevation, 8×9.5 mm in diameter with vitreous hemorrhage emanating from its surface. A scan revealed high regular internal reflectivity.

Case Information: A four-year-old boy was referred to the Division of Pediatric Ophthalmology at the Wilmer Eye Institute, Baltimore, Maryland for bilateral partial lens dislocation. Two months earlier, the patient had failed a vision screening at school and was referred for further evaluation. The child did not report any visual symptoms; however, the family observed that he would sit very close to the television and focus closely on toys. He had no history of trauma, developmental issues, or hearing deficits. Genetic screening at birth was normal. The family history was negative for ocular problems other than myopia in his mother. On initial ophthalmic examination, uncorrected visual acuity was 20/100 in the right eye and 20/250 in the left eye. Pupils were equally round and reactive to light, and intraocular pressure was normal by palpation. The child had no measurable stereopsis and suppression of his left eye on Worth 4-dot test. He was orthophoric at all distances. Examination revealed iridodenesis in both eyes and partially dislocated lenses; inferonasally in the right eye and inferiorly in the left eye. Cycloplegic refractive error was −14.50DS + 3.75DC x 005° in the right eye and −19.00 DS + 6.00 DC x 065° in the left eye. During a later examination under anesthesia, the macula in both eyes were within normal limits. Retinal vessels were normal without attenuation in both eyes. Peripheral exam was unremarkable in both eyes. Pachymetry measurements were 575 microns in the right eye and 584 microns in the left eye. Axial length was 21.83 mm in the right eye and 21.12 mm in the left eye. He was prescribed glasses and referred for a genetics evaluation. General physical examination found no evidence of any musculoskeletal features. Echocardiography revealed normal aortic dimensions. Genetic testing showed negative sequencing for deletion or duplication of fibrillin-1 (FBN-1) and cystathionine beta-synthase (CBS).
Diagnostic Tests: Slit-lamp examination was notable for iridodenesis in both eyes and partially dislocated lenses; inferonasally in the right eye and inferiorly in the left eye. Genetic testing showed negative sequencing for deletion or duplication of fibrillin-1 (FBN-1) and cystathionine beta-synthase (CBS). Echocardiography revealed normal aortic dimensions.

Case Information: A 38-year-old male was admitted to the Neurology Department at the Hillel Yaffe Medical Center with a severe headache lasting two days, accompanied by dizziness and confusion. Physical and neurological examinations were unremarkable. Brain CT scan results were normal. Cerebrospinal fluid analysis revealed a protein level of 110 mg/dL, glucose level of 66 mg/dL, presence of 2 lymphocytes, and negative results for oligoclonal bands. EEG indicated slight symmetric slowing of background activity. The patient received IV acyclovir treatment. Two days post-admission, persistent bradycardia with P wave changes on EKG was observed, lasting approximately two weeks. Cardiac transesophageal echocardiography showed normal results. Three days after admission, mild right-sided neurological signs were observed, including slight speech disturbance and reduced fluency. Brain CT angiography was normal. Five days later, the patient reported blurred vision in the right eye. Fundoscopy did not reveal arterial wall plaques. Visual field examination identified a small central scotoma in the right eye, and ocular coherence tomography showed inner retinal layer edema below the fovea.
Diagnostic Tests: Fluorescein angiography of the right eye disclosed central retinal artery branch occlusion.

Case Information: A 47-year-old male presented to the emergency department with complaints of blurred vision and pain in his left eye for the past four weeks. Initially, the patient attributed these symptoms to a headache or a previous condition related to his medical history of multiple sclerosis. Over time, his vision worsened, accompanied by the appearance of floaters and increased pain two weeks before seeking medical attention. Physical examination revealed a visual acuity of 20/60 in the left eye and a superior temporal field cut. The right eye, previously affected by vision loss, could only perceive light. Intraocular pressure was measured at 14 mm Hg in the left eye and 11 mm Hg in the right eye. The neurologic examination showed no other abnormalities. Ophthalmologic examination indicated left conjunctival injection and ciliary flush. A dilated ophthalmic examination identified peripheral retinal whitening in the superonasal area of the left eye, along with high-grade inflammation in the anterior chamber (3+ cell) and vitreous cavity (2+ cell).
Diagnostic Tests: Laboratory testing revealed a rapid plasma reagin titer of 1:256, with the patient testing negative for HIV. Ultrasonography of the eye revealed echogenic particles within the vitreous, with a possible undulating membrane that moved freely and swirled on dynamic exam. The patient’s retina was attached, and the diameter of the optic nerve was within normal limits.

Case Information: A 15-year-old female presented with pain on the left side of the abdomen and extended menstrual bleeding. She had a history of left nephrectomy at the age of 1 year due to a mass lesion, which was reported to be benign. A first-degree relative had a history of metastatic breast cancer at the age of 30 years. Physical examination revealed hirsutism. Imaging revealed a large mass in the left ovary. Surgical removal of the left ovary and fallopian tube was performed, and the specimen included a left ovarian tumor measuring 18 × 14 × 7 cm with a smooth surface.
Diagnostic Tests: Microscopic examination revealed nodular and diffuse growth of tumor cells with ovoid hyperchromatic nuclei, small nucleoli, amphophilic cytoplasm. Macrofollicle and microfollicle formations containing eosinophilic secretions were identified. The tumor cells were positive for steroidogenic factor 1 (SF-1) and inhibin, focally positive for cytokeratin (CK), and negative for SALL4. Reticulin stain highlighted groups/nests of tumor cells. B-catenin showed a positive membranous staining pattern. Pelvic magnetic resonance imaging revealed a pelvic mass measuring approximately 4.5 cm in axial diameter, located to the right of the rectum and probably originating from the right ovary. The tumor cells were positive for SF-1, B-catenin (membranous), alpha-inhibin, and calretinin and negative for SALL4, CK7, and epithelial membrane antigen (EMA).

Case Information: A three-year-old girl presented with severe abdominal pain, food refusal, constipation, and fever over the past seven days. She was born following a normal pregnancy and delivery, with non-consanguineous parents, and had a birth weight of 3130 g. Clinical examination revealed telecanthus, a prominent nasal bridge, a short philtrum, small hands, an anteriorized anus, severe psychomotor delay, absence of expressive language, and dysphagia. The main symptoms included persistent, inconsolable crying, abdominal distension, and mild fever. Blood tests showed moderate leukocytosis and abnormal electrolyte values. Urine cultures identified Escherichia (E.) coli pyelonephritis as the cause of fever and elevated white blood cell count. Antibiotic therapy was initiated, leading to the resolution of fever and leukocytosis. Despite the resolution of the urinary tract infection and normalization of blood values, the patient continued to experience abdominal bloating, severe agitation, constipation, and food refusal. Persistent crying due to abdominal distension was noted throughout the day.
Diagnostic Tests: Transabdominal ultrasound revealed fluid between the intestinal loops. Abdominal X-ray showed severe colic distension, causing diaphragmatic elevation.

Case Information: A 47-year-old male experienced hematochezia following a gastrointestinal infection. A colonoscopy revealed 23 polyps, with three located in the caecum and the remainder in the left colon. Polypectomy was conducted, and pathology of eight polyps indicated six tubular adenomas with low to moderate dysplasia and two tubulovillous adenomas, one of which exhibited severe dysplasia. The largest adenoma measured 20 mm × 8 mm × 15 mm. The patient had no family history of colonic adenomas or cancer, and no genetic testing was performed. The patient was placed under routine screening, and over a 10-year period (2007–2017), annual colonoscopic polypectomies removed approximately 40 polyps, with around eighty percent being adenomas. In June 2018, at age 58, a colonoscopy identified and removed 55 new polyps that had developed over the previous 6 months. Pathology described four of the five polyps as adenomas, with the remaining polyp identified as a sessile serrated polyp. The most recent colonoscopy in December 2018 revealed 20 polyps, all of which were tubular adenomas with low dysplasia. To date, the patient has developed 133 polyps and has declined a recommended colectomy.
Diagnostic Tests: A homozygous nonsense variant (NM_002528):c.268C>T, p. Gln90Ter in the NTHL1 gene was identified. No alterations were found in the other examined genes.

Case Information: A 57-year-old Caucasian male presented with acute pneumonia and progressive difficulty swallowing. He reported painless swallowing difficulties, dry mouth, hoarseness, and a sensation of a mass in the upper esophagus. His medical history includes type II diabetes, chronic bronchitis, chronic gastritis, urate nephropathy with a history of kidney stones, and coronary artery disease. The patient has a history of daily alcohol and nicotine use for 40 years. Physical examination revealed bilateral eyelid drooping and mild facial weakness. Observations included a wet voice and insufficient cough reflex after consuming solids and liquids, leading to aspiration. Laryngoscopy indicated incomplete glottic closure and impaired vocal cord mobility. A video-radiological barium examination showed aspiration during and after swallowing. Contrast-enhanced CT scans identified a homogeneous mass (1.5 × 2 cm) in the preepiglottic space, behind the hyoid bone. Panendoscopy and esophagus-gastroscopy were performed under general anesthesia. Endoscopic findings did not reveal any obvious cause for the progressive swallowing difficulty. A deep incision biopsy of the preepiglottic space was performed, showing only fatty tissue without any suspect structures. Histopathological evaluation confirmed the presence of fatty tissue without malignant pathology. Family history revealed that four of his eight siblings developed similar symptoms around the age of 50, with one brother experiencing only mild swallowing difficulty. Additionally, the patient's father, one paternal uncle, one paternal aunt, and her son have swallowing difficulties and eyelid drooping. The patient's family is of native German origin without French-Canadian or Jewish ancestry. The patient underwent bilateral eyelid surgery to correct drooping one year ago. Genetic counseling was initiated considering the family history of swallowing disorders.
Diagnostic Tests: DNA testing revealed a heterozygous (GCG)10 expansion of the (GCG)-mini-repeat, located in exon 1 of the poly(A) binding protein, nuclear 1gene (PABPN1).

Case Information: A 61-year-old Chinese male with a history of grade 1 hypertension reported experiencing right lower abdominal distention and intermittent upper abdominal pain for a duration of 4 months. Laboratory tests included serum creatinine (SCr), 24-hour 3-methyl-4-hydroxymandelic acid (VMA), adrenocorticotropic hormone (ACTH), sex hormone screening, plasma cortisol rhythm, and renin–angiotensin II–aldosterone system (RAAS) function in both upright and recumbent positions.
Diagnostic Tests: Ultrasonography showed a 4.4 cm × 3.4 cm hypoechoic nodule with clear boundaries and internal cord-like hyperechoic mass in the right hilum. Contrast-enhanced CT scan showed a round soft tissue nodule shadow in the right renal hilum with clear boundaries, uneven enhancement and a filling defect in the renal vein cavity. MRI showed a 4.2 × 3.2 × 3.5 cm mass with clear boundaries, slightly high DWI signal and significantly low ADC value.

Case Information: Mr. MT, a 32-year-old male, has been married for 11 years and has 5 children. He has no history of somatic or psychiatric conditions. He completed secondary school and works as a builder. He has no history of substance use except for smoking, which he quit 4 years ago. The patient was referred for psychiatric examination after consultations with urologists, neurologists, and general practitioners. A few minutes (10–15 minutes) after each ejaculation, he experiences intense fatigue, severe muscle, bone, and joint pain lasting 3–7 days. He also reports sneezing, eye redness, itching sensations throughout the body, and significant concentration difficulties. Additionally, he experiences temporary dental pain that resolves spontaneously. These symptoms occur with all forms of ejaculation, including nocturnal emission, masturbation, and vaginal ejaculation. The symptoms began at puberty (age 14) and have increased in severity and duration over time, initially lasting 3 days and now extending to 7 days, causing financial difficulties due to missed work. This has led to sexual avoidance behavior despite preserved sexual desire and normal erections. The frequency of sexual intercourse has decreased from twice a week to once a month. For the past 2 years, he has also experienced secondary premature ejaculation. On examination, the patient was in good general health, well-built, and had complete secondary sexual characteristics. His weight was 97 kg, height 180 cm, and blood pressure 120/80 mm/Hg. Clinical examinations, including neurological and urological assessments, were normal. Routine laboratory tests (CBC, renal function, blood glucose) and hormone levels (FT4, TSH, prolactin, cortisol, testosterone, DHEA) were within normal ranges.
Diagnostic Tests: The sperm freshly emitted from the patient was diluted to a concentration of 1: 40,000, then injected intracutaneously into the palmar surface of the left forearm, and compared to a cutaneous reaction to placebo with 0.9% intracutaneous saline. This test came back positive.

Case Information: A 50-year-old male presented with difficulty swallowing and a progressively enlarging, painless swelling in the left submandibular region over a period of 4 months. The mass had previously been drained and treated with a week-long course of narrow-spectrum antibiotics at an Ear Nose Throat clinic. Intraoral examination revealed a firm bulging of the left soft palate and left lateral pharyngeal wall, crossing the midline and displacing the uvula to the right, with smooth overlying mucosa. Digital palpation indicated that the left tonsil was firm. Despite the non-tender lesion causing significant difficulty swallowing, the patient reported no major complaints. He had no fever and did not experience throat soreness. The mass extended from the left side of the nasopharynx to the oropharynx, pushing the left tonsil towards the midline of the oropharynx. Externally, there was noticeable swelling in the left submandibular region. Clinical examination showed no involvement of cranial nerves.
Diagnostic Tests: CT and MRI scan showed homogenously enhancing tumour measuring 5 × 4 cm in the left parapharyngeal space. Fine needle aspiration cytology of the mass in the neck was consistent with benign mixed tumour.

Case Information: A 28-year-old male of mixed race has experienced scalp skin redundancy for two years. The condition is characterized by deep cerebriform folds and wrinkles, specifically in the parietal and occipital regions. The patient reports no comorbidities, no similar family history, no consanguinity, and no use of anabolic steroid drugs. Additionally, there is no history of skin or scalp inflammatory diseases. Neurological and ophthalmological examinations revealed no abnormalities.
Diagnostic Tests: The anatomopathological exam revealed epidermis and dermis within histological standards of normality. Skull X-ray, computed tomography of skull and sella turcica, nuclear magnetic resonance of the sella turcica and serum growth hormone dosage showed no alterations. TSH serum dosage, free T4, complete blood count, fasting blood glucose, total cholesterol and fractions, and Venereal Disease Research Laboratory test - VDRL were within normal limits.

Case Information: A 4-year-old girl presented with blue sclera and wrinkled skin. She was the only child of parents who were third-degree relatives (father aged 30 years, mother aged 24 years). She was delivered at term via LSCS with a birth weight of 2.25 kg. The perinatal period was uneventful. She exhibited motor developmental delay and mild learning difficulty. Physical examination revealed a weight of 12 kg (<3rd percentile), height of 97 cm (3rd-10th percentile), and head circumference of 44 cm (<3rd percentile). Notable features included palpebral down slant, bilateral epicanthal folds, blue sclera, flat nasal bridge, sagging cheeks, and prominent ears. She had generalized loose, wrinkled skin folds, especially on the face, neck, abdomen, and extremities. Systemic examinations were normal. Skeletal evaluation indicated bilateral hip dislocation. Ophthalmologic examination confirmed blue sclera and shallow anterior chambers. Echocardiography and abdominal ultrasonography results were normal. Isoelectric focusing for transferrin showed mildly elevated levels of A-, mono-, and di-sialotransferrin, with slightly reduced levels of tetra-sialotransferrin.
Diagnostic Tests: Mutation analysis showed mutations c. 826-2A > G in intron 9 and c. 1973_1976del (p.Val660LeufsX682) in exon 16 of the ATP6V0A2 gene in a compound heterozygous state.
